Goethe was simply such a great poet—the greatest poet—that he had to become the founder of a cult.
But he diverted this necessity into the individualistic world of educated culture, and everyone followed him there as well.

The final result: the beautiful animal, and the image presented by the self-conscious “elite” that came to power in Germany in 1936. That was the end of a road prepared, among others, by an honest Englishman, H. S. Chamberlain, and an honest Jew, Otto Weininger.
I have often had the impression of a theogony—a theogony ab ovo, from the very beginning, so to speak.

There is no question that we are standing at the beginning of a theogonic age, an age in which new gods are being made. That is why there is such great anticipation surrounding your work on Prometheus. For my part, I still remain with my contemplation of the Christian Epimetheus:
The more that meaning seeks itself, The more the soul is led from dark captivity Out into the world. Do what you must! It has always already been done; You only give an answer.

Gilles said in 1942: no longer Prometheus, whose reign is over, but a pure primal melody—Orpheus. We really are living through a theogony, provided we accept the concept of nihilism and refuse simply to stop there.
Däubler’s work is likewise a theogony.
Positivist science: an especially brazen theogony of “we shall make it ourselves.”
“The point is to change the world”: again, the makers of gods. And every time, this new theogony ends with a new elite.
Better, then, to stick with the old elites we already know!
Though of course these gentlemen of refined taste need protection themselves.

“Only when a majority loaded a minority with the full weight of its own repressed aggression could it regard itself as free from aggression, and therefore as good and just. Only then did it create a good conscience for itself and gain the moral upper hand, from which those parts of society that had remained at the level of primitive, unrepressed aggression could no longer escape.”

Paul Reiwald, The Conquest of Peace: Psychological Foundations of the New Society, Zurich and New York, Europa Verlag, 1944, pp. 99–100; quoted by Hans Wehberg in the essay “Peaceful and Aggressive States: The Problem of International Criminal Law” (Die Friedenswarte, 1944, p. 25).
Humanity’s enemy number one is the state of tension created by mass situations—not merely legal or political disputes. Such tensions can only be tamed. They cannot be eradicated.
Aggression is released against the criminal in order to redirect it toward another target.
Criminals are those who have achieved no repression at all, or only very little.
So the starting point is this:
Human beings are aggressive by nature. And the collective is even more so—the “great man,” the μάκρος ἄνθρωπος, humanity writ large.

I can tell from even the briefest and most casual discussion of natural law—and all the more from any serious and detailed discussion—whether the author knows Hegel’s essay “The Scientific Ways of Treating Natural Law” (1802/03).
If he does not, I recommend that he read it.
Unless, that is, the discussion itself reveals that the author is simply incapable of understanding Hegel.
In that unfortunately very common case, I stop reading.
Why is this young Hegel of 1802 so overwhelmingly great? And why is the old Hegel—for example, the Hegel of the 1828 essay on Hamann’s writings—so narrow, unfair, and determined to be right?
The parallel with Goethe is obvious.
Of course, the old Goethe played the role of cult image with more taste, with more effective means of cultivating the cult, and therefore with greater success than the old Hegel.
Strange how, only a few weeks ago, the thought of the Deus absconditus, the hidden God, tormented me (see 6 December 1947).
Today Bilfinger writes, in a letter dated 18 December:

“The Deus absconditus has lowered the Iron Curtain. Incidentally: the hidden God occupies me a great deal. I also have literature on the subject, probably connected with Persian religious ideas. But the Christmas message, our hymns, Beethoven, all of it—who can take that away from us?”
And while this mixture of religion with the comforts of cultivated culture still bothers me, I myself sit here playing the Meistersinger and committing the worst sins of cultivated culture.
I found this in Lucan, Book VII:
“We lie when we say Jupiter reigns.”

German soil, which fate has held beneath perpetual tyrants. Among the peoples who endure kings, ours is the lowest lot, we who are ashamed to serve. Surely no gods watch over us, since the ages are swept away by blind chance. We lie when we say Jupiter reigns. Will freedom never return? This is the deeply moving lament of collapse. And from precisely this depth of nihilism, Christianity rises.
Still thinking about the passage in Lucan, VII, 440–460. What does this mean:
“Civil wars will make gods equal to those above”?
(For a moment I thought it said divis rather than divos.)
Human beings are aggressive by nature.
Reiwald discovers that defence is the best form of attack. Only then does the dialectic of war reach its full intensity.
The idea that attack is the best defence now seems naïvely direct, almost unsophisticated.
To defend yourself, by contrast—to make the opponent appear to be the attacker—is rational and civilized. This dialectic of psychological repression produces the higher logic of higher imperialism.
The more disciplined the individual becomes, the more aggressive the collective becomes.

The reason is that the individual can now satisfy his own aggression indirectly, as a member of the mass. So the “great man”—the collective, the state—is also the great aggressor. It becomes the reservoir into which everything irrational flows.
Rational within, and therefore all the more irrational without.
Compare my Leviathan, p. 75, on relations between collective bodies. This is the unavoidable machinery created by the rationalization of the individual.
Meter belongs to magic. But there must remain a certain amount of open space between the meter and the thought or subject matter expressed by the poem.
Put crudely: between form and content there is still an empty space. And in that interval, in that space which remains empty, the numinous—the mysterious sense of sacred presence—begins to resonate.
Goethe’s poem “To the Moon” shows this beautifully.
In Däubler there is too much noise made by the sounds of words and by great clusters of words.
The numinous element in a poem is not the sound itself. It resonates in the empty space. It is not itself emptiness, τὸ κενόν. It moves within emptiness.
Empty space is the condition that makes movement possible. But the numinous has a special relationship to emptiness.
The emptier the vessel, the purer it is.
Meter is the empty vessel not for the content, but for the magical vibration.
To H. Bung, on the repeated confusion between me and my namesake in Tübingen:
I am still not sure whether these mix-ups help or hinder my great ambition to achieve perfect obscurité and complete self-effacement.
But, having learned from Reiwald, I can imagine that they have something usefully distracting about them.
Perhaps they disarm the most direct and primitive form of aggression.
(Then a question about Wehberg’s essay and its discussion of C. S.)
In any case, you must not imagine my situation as though I were rummaging around in the decaying printer’s ink of the past.
A great deal of it may be blown into my face, but I have not allowed my thoughts to be turned backward.
Most of what people are thinking today, insofar as it is new and interesting, we already thought in advance.
And whatever is worth thinking over afterward—in the manner of Epimetheus—we have thought over.
Mrs Schmitt really has managed to set up a home here.
Gilles’s fish, Nay’s Leviathan, Nay’s magnificent diamond—all of them surround me again.
Like a submarine that continually reassembles itself, I make my submarine, subterranean, sublunary journey through fire and water.
Three times the Leviathan has swallowed me and then spat me out again. Now I understand the three chapters of the Book of Jonah.
Strange, by contrast, how theogonic writings are flowing toward me from every direction:
G. Nebel; the Greek gods of Fr.[iedrich] G.[eorg] J.[ünger]; Däubler’s Hymns to Italy and the Attic Sonnets.
I look out at a magnificent mountain. Behind it lies another landscape, different from the Lennetal valley where I live.
The river outside my window is splendid in winter. It looks as though it has just come into existence, without a past and without a future: pure Heraclitean present.
I am reading Troeltsch’s The Social Teachings of the Christian Churches (1912), especially this sentence (p. 173):

“The Christian theory of natural law—in which the pure natural law of humanity’s original condition, the entirely opposite relative natural law of humanity’s fallen condition, positive law which often contains the most terrible atrocities, and theocratic supreme authority, which despite all natural law claims to communicate true goodness from itself, are constantly colliding—is pitiful and confused as a scientific theory. But as a practical doctrine it is of the highest importance in the history of culture and society. It is the Church’s true cultural dogma, and as such it is at least (!) as important as the dogma of the Trinity or the other major dogmas.”
This Troeltsch would have understood me, just as I understand him. How alone I am, then!

The theological concept that truly corresponded to his political theory would have been the κατέχων, the katechon, the restraining power. Instead he wandered into this labyrinth of absolute and relative natural law!
There is a very simple sociological explanation for the hopelessness of Charles Péguy’s complaint that he could find no success among Catholics.
Perhaps the Jesuit order was the κατέχων. But what about after 1814?
